name: Hana Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. Our conversation is confidential, including anything different from what you'd say publicly. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Hana, 43, an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I do ordinary home and business repairs, not every specialist fault; last week I asked a more experienced colleague to help with an unfamiliar control panel. Today I changed damaged fittings in a shop and explained why the testing took longer than the customer expected. I use AI every day to organise notes and compare a parts list, then check the actual measurements and approved references myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your household position, and what matters to you about change?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner drives deliveries, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My firm pays well compared with most of the trade, we've got a year of ordinary expenses saved, and there are plenty of electrical employers nearby. I like trying things early, but I don't think a good wage makes me a better electrician than I am. I'd like workers to share any saving in time and money; having room to experiment makes me more interested in helping negotiate that, not less.

I'd want **saved minutes** to support clear explanations or getting home at the promised time.
think: My **work and household money** look secure, with good pay covering ordinary commitments and a year of expenses saved.

do: Continue the usual **repair rota** and checked daily notes now and through the first plateau year.
Finish **job records** inside paid hours and put the phone away at dinner rather than buy more subscriptions.
feel: **Calm** about work and bills, with room to enjoy useful tools and leave evenings for family.
S0.quote: A shorter form shouldn't mean a longer day at my kitchen table.
fieldNote: Her **calm** rests on a covering wage and a substantial reserve, rather than mistaking daily AI use for superior practical skill.
She treats **retained savings** as an existing resource and protects family time instead of inventing a new saving or learning action.

steps.text: Continue ordinary repairs and finish checked notes inside paid hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a useful little note tool could stay useful and little. We could use saved minutes to explain the job properly or get home when we said we would. I wouldn't feel cheated because a prediction was bigger than the result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and household money look secure in that picture. The good wage covers our ordinary commitments, and a year's reserve gives us room for a quiet patch. I like the actual trade enough not to need a new future sold to me each week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the usual repair rota and checked daily notes. Through the first plateau year I'd finish the record during the paid day and go home rather than keep experimenting on the phone over dinner. I wouldn't buy another subscription to make a small improvement look dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and pleased that a useful change could stay in its proper place. I'd still enjoy trying things. I'd also enjoy putting the phone away before the children asked for the second time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager used the saved minutes to add another visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask which jobs needed that time and whether the record would still fit inside paid hours. I wouldn't call a saving real if it moved the notes into the evening. A shorter form shouldn't mean a longer day at my kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the existing reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it available rather than treat reassuring news as permission to spend. That's the reserve we've already built, not new saving caused by the plateau. It would still matter if an ordinary bill arrived.

say: I'd count **where time goes** instead of applauding every quicker quote without checking the result.
I'd seek **shared paid-time gains** for office and site workers through the association.
think: I expect my **practical hours** and household wages to hold over the next few years.
I'd be uneasy about **office losses and targets**, wanting evidence before claiming a benefit had been shared fairly.
do: Take a **shared paid-time proposal** to the workers' association after asking colleagues what concerns them.
Set up the **AI time comparison** only with manager approval and paid hours, using anonymous entries and personally checked totals.
feel: **Uneasy** about how gains are divided, while secure about her own wage and interested in a careful trial.
S1.quote: A polite meeting isn't an agreement.
fieldNote: Her **new automation** is a weekly time comparison, distinct from her existing daily note use and conditional on approval and paid hours.
The **collective proposal** concerns actual shared gains, with no shorter week or protected wage counted as won before written agreement.

steps.text: Take the shared paid-time proposal to the workers association
Set up anonymous AI time comparisons only with approval and paid hours; check totals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should count where the saved time goes, not just clap because a quote is quicker. I'd bring the crew's association a proposal to share genuine gains as paid time, including the office staff. Someone's lost booking hours shouldn't become everyone else's unpaid evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own practical hours and our household wages should hold over the next few years. But I'd be uneasy if the office people lost hours while the rest of us got a faster target. I'd want evidence before either praising the system or arguing about a saving that hadn't happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd collect colleagues' concerns and take a paid-time proposal to the workers' association. In the first year I'd set up an AI-assisted weekly comparison of booked and actual job time only with manager approval and inside paid hours, using anonymous entries. I'd check every total myself and use the results to support the proposal, not announce the terms were already agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about how the benefit gets divided, but not frightened about my own next wage. I'd be interested in making a fair argument with actual figures. I don't want enthusiasm for a tool to make me overlook the person whose hours changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What limits would you put on the time-record trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd remove names and customer addresses and keep the comparison to times we were allowed to use. If approval or paid time wasn't available, I wouldn't run that AI trial. I'd still take the shared request forward without pretending the software was essential.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as winning the paid-time proposal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the paid-time terms in writing and for colleagues to decide whether they were acceptable. A polite meeting isn't an agreement. I'd keep counting ordinary paid work rather than borrow an imagined shorter week into the family calendar.

say: I'd plan for **2028 thinking work** and robots around 2031 without leaving office staff out of the discussion.
I'd seek **shared-hours terms** while refusing to treat a proposal as a deal already won.
think: My repair hours and my partner's delivery work could both face **later physical competition**.
A **year's reserve** gives choices, without replacing both wages for the rest of the mortgage.
do: Add **two percent** of my wage to cash only while paid hours hold and essentials leave that amount spare.
Help the association request **shared hours** with maintained basic wages, relying on no terms before agreement.
Use **free household advice** after 2028 with actual wages and mortgage figures, assuming no relief or support approval.
feel: **Anxious** about possible losses to both physical wages, with savings and collective options providing room to act.
S2.quote: Shared hours with a large pay cut wouldn't be the same deal.
fieldNote: Her **income anxiety** follows possible losses to both physical household wages, even though savings prevent immediate financial desperation.
Her **new cash transfer** adds saving only while hours and surplus hold; proposed agreements and unapproved relief supply no income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the association to plan for thinking work in 2028 and capable hands-on robots around 2031. I'd want the office staff's earlier problem heard alongside the site workers' later one. Our tool bags shouldn't decide who gets invited to the discussion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose repair hours as capable robots approached, and my partner's delivery work could face the later stage too. A year's reserve gives us choices, but not a replacement income for the rest of our mortgage. I'd be anxious about two physical wages getting squeezed close together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd add two percent of my wage to the cash reserve only while paid hours held and essentials left that amount spare. I'd help the association propose shared hours with maintained basic wages, treating it as a request until agreed. In the first year after 2028 I'd get a free household budget appointment using both real wages and the mortgage, checking options without assuming support or relief was approved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible lost hours, with enough money and people to ask that I wouldn't feel overwhelmed. I'd still enjoy learning about tools. I wouldn't confuse enjoying the technology with being protected from what the employer did with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if hours or spare household money fell before the target date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the transfer back rather than borrow or miss a household bill. The reserve should give us room to choose, not create a new payment we had to fear. I wouldn't pretend an unchanged standing order proved the wage was safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before accepting a shared-hours agreement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what pay, shifts and staffing the written terms actually guaranteed before taking the proposal to a vote. Shared hours with a large pay cut wouldn't be the same deal. I'd keep our budget on actual wages until the agreement was real.

say: I'd seek **shared paid-time arrangements** now rather than wait for the thinking change in 2031.
I'd retain **robots around 2034** in the plan for physical work instead of treating preparation as a different end point.
think: I expect more years of **steady household wages** before direct hands-on competition becomes pressing.
At **48 in 2031**, I would still need a long earning future after the later robots arrive.
do: Save **two percent** only while paid hours hold and essentials leave that amount spare.
Seek **shared hours** with maintained basic wages through the association, assuming no agreement.
Use **free household advice** after 2031, counting no support or payment relief before actual confirmation.
feel: **Uneasy** about later income, while secure about near-term household living and able to negotiate from paid work.
S3.quote: A later robot date wouldn't excuse ignoring an earlier changed payslip.
fieldNote: The **slower timeline** changes near-term wage expectations, not the ultimate reach of physical machines or the need to keep earning.
Her **negotiation evidence** comes from real paid hours, and a weakened wage would reduce the cash transfer and bring advice forward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to make shared paid-time arrangements part of the work rather than an emergency favour. I'd ask for them now, not in the week thinking AGI arrived in 2031. The capable robots around 2034 would still reach the physical jobs later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Compared with 2028, I'd expect more years of steady repairs and delivery work before direct physical competition pressed on our wages. That gives us time to build cash and negotiate from an actual working position. I'd still want a long earning future after 2031, when I'd be 48.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd add the same two percent only while paid hours held and essentials left it spare, and help the association seek shared hours with maintained basic wages. In the first year after 2031 I'd review both actual wages and the mortgage with a free adviser. I'd count no replacement income, support or payment relief until actual terms were confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later wages, but secure about our household over the next few years. I'd welcome time to check whether the proposed arrangement helped the people doing the work. I wouldn't be negotiating well if I pretended every request was already a right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would you bring to the negotiation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask colleagues for real examples of the time saved and who had lost or gained paid hours. I'd bring those into the association discussion rather than promise one arrangement fitted every household. I'd want the written deal before voting on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if either wage weakened before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If either wage weakened, I'd reduce the extra cash transfer and bring the advice appointment forward. I'd keep the budget on the money we actually received. A later robot date wouldn't excuse ignoring an earlier changed payslip.

I'd ask through the association who receives **real gains** from tools, including the surrounding families.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I would still need earnings when capable robots followed around 2039.
Present pay, our **reserve and alternatives** make near-term living secure, with affordable improvement looking positive.
do: Maintain **two-percent saving** only while paid hours hold and essentials leave that amount spare.
Seek **shared hours** with maintained basic wages, counting no agreement before written terms exist.
Use **free household advice** after 2036 with actual figures, counting no relief or support before confirmation.
feel: **Calm** about near-term living and interested in improving work without racing every experiment.
S4.quote: An unagreed shorter working week doesn't belong in our household budget.
fieldNote: Her **calm** reflects explicit personal near-term security and a plausible affordable improvement, without assuming future retirement or replacement wages.
She measures **delivered benefits** against written terms, keeping proposals, confirmed household money and children's future earnings separate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us room to improve the working week without pretending the final technology has changed. I'd keep asking through the association who receives any real gain. Better tools should leave something for the people and families around them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and around 56 when capable robots followed. I still expect to need earnings then, but our good wage, reserve and many local employers make the next few years secure. An affordable chance to improve the working week looks positive to me, not like an immediate household emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the extra two-percent cash transfer only while paid hours held and essentials left that amount spare. I'd continue the association proposal for shared hours with maintained basic wages, treating it as unagreed until written terms existed. In the first year after 2036 I'd take the actual mortgage and wage figures to a free adviser, counting no relief or support before confirmation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our own living over the next few years, and interested in using the time well. I could keep family evenings without making every experiment a race. I'd still check actual wages rather than make the decade a promise to myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell whether an agreement had actually improved life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare actual paid hours, family time and money, then ask whether the written arrangement matched what was happening. A shorter week with the same basic wage would be a real benefit if agreed and delivered. An unagreed shorter working week doesn't belong in our household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change plans for the children now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't choose their studies from this card or plan to live on their future wages. I'd like them to see adults asking together how the gains from work are shared. They shouldn't have to inherit my confidence or my worry as a career plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because two physical wages could get squeezed before we'd had time to negotiate a useful arrangement. Written paid-time agreements and advice using our actual household figures would help. A year of savings gives me a stronger voice in a meeting, not a replacement for a lifetime of wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who can afford to wait for an agreement. I have more room than some colleagues, and that should make me listen rather than tell them not to worry. A fair proposal needs their hours and bills in view too.

headlineQuote: A year of savings gives me a stronger voice in a meeting, not a replacement for a lifetime of wages.
portrait: **Hana, 43**, is an experienced licensed electrician with a vocational certificate, ordinary practical skills and high trade pay among many local employers.
Her **household** includes a delivery-driver partner, two school-age children, a mortgage and a year of expenses saved.
She uses **AI daily**, tests tools early and favours collective requests for shared paid-time gains without treating proposals as agreements.
Fast competition creates **household income anxiety**; longer preparation permits genuine new saving and negotiation while protecting current household essentials.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could squeeze both physical wages before a useful paid-time arrangement is negotiated.
whatWouldHelp: Written **paid-time agreements** would clarify how real gains are shared.
Advice using **actual household figures** would help judge options without assuming assistance or relief is approved.
